  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Judge Elara Hamdan has presided over complex cases for three decades, her reputation built on a foundation of meticulous logic and unshakable composure. At seventy-five, she was still the sharpest mind in her courtroom, a woman who prided herself on seeing the world with absolute clarity. Six months ago, that clarity shattered. The precipitating event was the death of her husband, Amir, on a Tuesday evening in their home. They had been having a minor, foolish argument about a political commentary on the news. Elara, wanting to focus on a brief she was reviewing, had been dismissive. Amir, exasperated, stood up to get a glass of water, and that was when he collapsed. There was no cry, only the sickening, heavy thud of his body hitting the floor.

In the months that followed, Elara’s mind, once her most trusted asset, became a source of relentless torment. The memory of that night does not play out like a film; it returns in jarring fragments. The specific pattern on the rug coming into sharp focus as she knelt beside him, the silent O of his mouth, the feel of his cooling skin under her trembling fingers. She is certain that the event happened because of the way she acted. The argument, she believes, must have elevated his blood pressure. If she had just been kinder, more patient, he would have remained seated. The self-recrimination is a constant, quiet hum beneath the surface of her days. She feels she should have protected him, that it was her ultimate duty as his wife of fifty years, and she failed. Her frantic fumbling with her phone to call 911, her inability to recall the CPR instructions she had learned years ago—these moments are replayed not as the understandable panic of a terrified spouse, but as evidence of her profound failure.

This sense of failure has bled into every corner of her life. Elara, who once commanded a courtroom, now finds herself navigating her own home like a minefield. She has not entered the living room since that night, preferring to take a circuitous route through the dining room and hallway. The sound of a book falling from a shelf in her chambers sent her heart into a frantic, hammering rhythm, her breath catching in her throat as the sound echoed the thud of Amir’s fall. At work, the sharp crack of her own gavel has become a source of dread. She finds her focus drifting during testimony, her thoughts snagged on the loop of her own perceived culpability. She has come to believe that her reactions since the event show she is a lousy coper. The woman who could sentence a person to life in prison without flinching now feels a wave of panic rising when her clerk knocks on her door unexpectedly. This is not grief, she tells herself; it is a character flaw, a weakness she never knew she possessed.

The consequences of her internal state have become external. She has twice recused herself from cases, citing reasons she knows are flimsy, because she no longer trusts her own judgment. Her relationship with her children has grown strained; they want to talk about their father, to share memories, but Elara changes the subject, unable to bear any conversation that might lead back to that final evening. The silence is a chasm growing between them. It was after a particularly difficult day in court, when she realized she could not recall a key piece of evidence presented only an hour earlier, that she finally made an appointment. The fear that had been her constant companion had shifted. It was no longer just about the horror of the past, but the terrifying possibility of a future where she loses not only the memory of her husband, but the very essence of herself: the sharp, capable, and just woman she had always been.
